stories.title: Nurses and midwives to protest at hospitals over pay
stories.summary: Members of the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) will hold lunchtime protests at hospitals across the country over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal. It comes ahead of planned strikes by public sector workers on 14 October and 21 October. "INMO members will be protesting over cost-of-living measures and the impact it is having on staffing in work locations," the union said in a statement. Since last week, workers across the public sector have been engaging in industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule. Unions have accused the Government of failing to make meaningful commitments on pay following the expiration of the last public sector agreement at the end of June. On Tuesday, the Government announced that funding of €1.2 billion has been allocated in the Budget for a public sector pay deal.

stories.title: Endometriosis survey finds 14-year average wait for diagnosis
stories.summary: Some women in Ireland with endometriosis are waiting over 14 years for an official diagnosis, new data has revealed. The finding is among a series of stark statistics contained in a national survey of patients' experience of endometriosis care in Ireland. Endometriosis is a debilitating inflammatory disease where tissue similar to the inner lining of the uterus grows in other parts of the body causing pain, inflammation and scar tissue. "If it's caused fibrosis and there are nodules of endometriosis, particularly behind the womb, that can cause significant pain during intercourse," added Dr Bainton, who specialises in endometriosis care and surgery. "If it's growing near the bowel then we often see painful defecation as a symptom. Similarly, if it’s affecting the bladder and the urinary tract, it can cause frequency of going to the lavatory and it can cause pain when passing urine. And if we're seeing it outside the pelvis, it can start to affect other structures. "If it's growing in the lungs, it can grow on the diaphragm, you can get pain in the shoulder, pain the chest and difficulty breathing, particularly during menstruation when the endometriosis is also bleeding."

stories.title: Govt 'tried to get balance' in budget spending - McEntee
stories.summary: Senior Government figures have defended the spending plans announced in Budget 2027, despite sharp criticism from the State's financial watchdog and opposition politicians. The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (IFAC) accused the coalition of playing "fast and loose" with the public finances, putting them on a worse trajectory. "The Government should be saving more, making its tax base more secure, and avoiding aimless drift" IFAC added in a statement. Minster for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee responded, saying: "There's people saying we spent too much, people saying not enough". She told reporters in Dublin that the Government had "tried to get a balance". The coalition has "invested in people and services", Ms McEntee said, including Income Tax changes, Carbon Tax policies and new plans to help people retrofit their homes.

stories.title: Tesco raises profit outlook floor after first-half rise
stories.summary: Supermarket group Tesco has today lifted the bottom end of its full-year profit outlook after reporting a 6.5% increase for its first half, even as a very hot summer weighed on sales volumes across the industry. The group said it made an adjusted operating profit of £1.783 billion ($2.35 billion) for the 26 weeks to August 29, on sales, excluding VAT sales tax and fuel, up 2% to £33.8 billion. Tesco said its like for likes sales in Ireland rose by 4.1% to £1.666 billion, adding that it has a market share of 24.1% - an increase of 44 basis points on the back of strong like-for-like sales growth and new space openings. It said that strong volume growth across both Fresh and Packaged continued to drive food like-for-like sales in Ireland, which grew 4.4%. Food growth was further supported by a strong Tesco Finest performance, which saw growth of 12.8% compared to the same time last year. It noted like-for-like sales growth across all channels, with Online seeing the fastest growth of 11.9% year-on-year. Its Whoosh delivery service is now available in 47 stores, contributing 1.9ppts to overall Online growth. Tesco said its Irish large stores' like-for-like sales grew 3.3% as it continued to maintain a competitive price position in the market, while Convenience grew 3.1%. Non-food sales grew 1.5% on a like-for-like basis, with a strong performance in Home, supported by volume growth, it added.

stories.title: Israeli strikes kill 3 in Gaza on 7 October anniversary
stories.summary: Israel carried out new strikes in Gaza as it marked the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks by Hamas, with Palestinian officials reporting three people dead. Loud bangs across the border in Gaza were audible from the site of the Nova music festival just as family members gathered at dawn to mourn the more than 300 people killed three years earlier. On 7 October 2023, Palestinian fighters breached the border, storming southern Israel with gunfire, rockets and grenades. A total of 1,221 people died in the attack, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures. Militants also took 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead. In Gaza City, Al-Shifa hospital reported two people killed in an Israeli strike overnight.

stories.title: Stapleton flourishing at Foxes after finding her 'home'
stories.summary: Jessie Stapleton has been a Swiss Army knife for the Republic of Ireland and a gun for hire at club level. The 21-year-old is a versatile operator, particularly comfortable at centre-half but very capable at the base of midfield. It's her misfortune - and probably the source of personal frustration - that Carla Ward has a stack of options in those positions, diluting Stapleton's involvement over the past year. But a permanent move to Leicester City should help the Dubliner to strenghthen her case as the quest to reach next year's World Cup in Brazil comes to the boil. Stapleton is in Astana with the squad ahead of Friday's World Cup play-off semi-final first leg against Kazakhstan. Since moving to West Ham from Shelbourne in 2023, she's been a bit of a nomad. Loan spells at Reading, Sunderland and Nottingham Forest offered game time, but Stapleton could never bed down at a club to fully realise her potential.

stories.title: Divilly, O'Shea and Mackin in running for Players' POTY
stories.summary: Galway's All-Ireland winner Olivia Divilly, Kerry captain Síofra O’Shea and Armagh forward Aimee Mackin are the nominees for the 2026 TG4 Players’ Player of the Year Award. The winner will be revealed at the All-Star Awards banquet at The Bonnington Dublin Hotel on Saturday, 14 November. It is the second successive year that Divilly has been nominated for the accolade – Dublin’s Hannah Tyrrell was last year’s winner – and marks another stellar year with the Tribes. Divilly finished the championship with a tally of 2-27, including three points in the final against Kerry as Galway landed the Brendan Martin Cup for the first time since 2004. O’Shea, meanwhile, registered five points for runners-up Kerry in the showpiece decider, and her overall haul of 3-30 saw her finish as top scorer in the championship. Armagh’s season ended at the semi-final stage but Mackin was majestic nevertheless for the Orchard County.

stories.title: Duffy: 'We've had our downs - we've turned it around'
stories.summary: Nearing the end of a turbulent campaign, Derry City look to have found their form in time to mount another tilt for FAI Cup glory, with Galway United standing in the way of a third final appearance in the 2020s. In a stark reminder of what a chaotic and messy season it had been for Derry for so long, their pre-semi-final press conference was preceded by the appearance of a PFAI press release issued on behalf of James McClean, in which the Republic of Ireland centurion hit out at his "incomprehensible" treatment from his hometown club. The statement evidently caught Derry City by surprise, the club pointedly noting in their response that "it was made without prior notice to the club, just four days before the biggest match of the club's season." Interim manager Mark Connolly, who has not selected McClean for any competitive matchday squads since his appointment in early August, said he had just seen the statement for the first time this morning and wasn't inclined to comment publicly on the matter. "Obviously, I've seen it this morning when we were heading into training," Connolly said. "James had acknowledged that he didn't want to be a public thing and that's the way I work. We just want to keep everything in-house and my full focus is on Saturday's game."

stories.title: Belfast defeat 'etched in the memory' of McMillan
stories.summary: Munster will be without Michael Milne, Fineen Wycherley and Diarmuid Kilgallen for Saturday's URC interpro against Ulster in Belfast, although head coach Clayton McMillan is confident of getting a couple of those players back for their Champions Cup opener against Racing 92 next week. Loosehead prop Milne suffered an ankle injury in the early stages of Saturday's 26-22 win against the Bulls, while wing Kilgallen injured his hamstring in the act of scoring a try, and second row Wycherley missed out due to a shoulder issue. Kilgallen’s injury appears to be the most serious, with McMillan guessing the 26-year-old could miss a few weeks of action, but he is optimistic that Milne and Wycherley's injuries could be healed in time for the visit of Racing to Cork next week. "Michael Milne's looked quite nasty, the way that he was folded in a tackle, but it's actually been pretty good," the head coach said. "I don't imagine that his time out is going to be much at all. Potentially a good chance of being back involved next week [against Racing 92]. "Diarmuid Kilgallen, still early days, but probably thinking at least two to three weeks.

stories.title: Visions of a city under pressure - Eoghan Quinn's new play
stories.summary: Director Claire O'Reilly introduces visions, a timely new play from acclaimed playwright Eoghan Quinn receiving its world premiere on the Peacock stage at the Abbey Theatre, as part of this year's Dublin Theatre Festival. Eoghan has written a play that's funny, political, mercurial, and deeply human. I’ve loved exploring its beguiling world, and I’m delighted to share it with you. Staged in the Peacock and set down the road, the 'why now’ of visions is palpable and personal. I’m a born and bred Dubliner, a city where dereliction, redevelopment, housing, heritage, ownership, and questions of the future and who it’s for are all very much alive, and answered in part by an undercurrent of unrest and eruptions of violence. Dublin is a city under pressure, at a time when our capacity to imagine is becoming less practised, and more algorithmically outsourced. But as well as grappling with these truths, visions consistently foregrounds complex, yearning and hilarious people. I hope it leaves you with the teasing, tantalising feeling of possibility.

stories.title: Why Irish designers are so drawn to the Gothic in fashion
stories.summary: Laura Fitzachary is a historian and historical content creator based in Dublin who specialises in fashion and beauty history in Ireland and beyond. Ahead of spooky season, fashion historian Laura Fitzachary explores how Gothic tropes and traditional Irish stories have Irish fashion designers enthralled. Inspired by storytelling and craftsmanship, Gothic fashion naturally finds a home in Ireland. So it is not surprising that Irish designers such as Jonathan Anderson, Dior Creative Director, and Simone Rocha have referenced Gothic literature, Irish mythology and Victorian mourning dress. A literal take on the iconic Dior Book Tote was revealed by Magherafelt-born Anderson in 2025 in the lead up Dior Homme SS '26, one of which featured an homage to the first edition of Dracula by Bram Stoker. As noted by Dior, Stoker’s Dracula take its place in Anderson’s "dream library". The Gothic horror novel was published in 1897 and draws extensively from folklore and history. While there are several theories as to who the character of 'Dracula’ is based on, this mystery has even spilled over into fashion. Alexander McQueen’s FW ‘09 Menswear featured models bearing a cane, a top hat and a coat draped over the shoulders – a direct nod to the human form of the vampire depicted by Gary Oldman in Bram Stoker’s Dracula, Francis Ford Coppola's 1992 interpretation of the novel. What is known is the strong influence of traditional Irish tales on Stoker’s writing, which has been argued by historians such as David J. Skal.

stories.title: €20m extra needed by An Garda Síochána last year
stories.summary: Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly has said the force needed an extra €20 million last year - in addition to its allocation of €2.3 billion - because of additional recruits and the need to respond to significant operational demands. These included increased protest activity and the major policing and security operation associated with the visit of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in December. Mr Kelly will tell the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee today that the funding supported continued investment in personnel, equipment, technology and operational capability. The vast majority of An Garda Síochána's budget is spent on pay, which increased by 4% last year, because of the implementation of a national pay agreement and an increase in garda numbers. The fleet - of 3,650 - is the highest it has been, including 300 electric vehicles. An Garda Síochána bought new cars, a plane, helicopters, an armoured vehicle for the emergency and armed response units, equipment for public order units and rigid hull inflatable boats for the Water Unit.

stories.title: School secretaries, caretakers vote to accept proposals
stories.summary: School secretaries and caretakers, who are members of the Fórsa trade union, have voted overwhelmingly to accept proposals on pay, pensions and employment conditions. Among the measures are the implementation of a Labour Court recommendation on pension lump sums and gratuity payments, improved sick leave arrangements, paid bereavement leave and a new pay structure for school caretakers. Caretakers will receive backdated pay to March 2026 and move, by March next year, to a pay scale aligned with that applying to Education and Training Board caretakers. The recommendations follow a dispute which saw around 2,600 school secretaries and caretakers engage in strike action for over a week at the start of the school year last year, impacting around 2,000 schools. "The result reflects the commitment and solidarity of school secretaries and caretakers throughout a lengthy and challenging process," said Fórsa Head of Education Andy Pike. "A 94% vote in favour, on a turnout of more than 88%, is a very strong endorsement of these proposals," Mr Pike said.

stories.title: Budget puts public finances on a 'worse trajectory'
stories.summary: The spending watchdog, the Fiscal Advisory Council, has criticised Budget 2027, saying it puts public finances on a "worse trajectory". In its release on Budget 2027, entitled 'Fast and Loose', it said that this is due to "repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax". The independent statutory body said spending has grown much faster than planned. "Spending increases net of tax measures have been running at a blistering pace. "But governments have since budgeted for 6%, before actually delivering about 10%, double the speed limit. In its flash analysis, the Fiscal Council said the Government is continuing to use high-risk receipts to fund permanent tax and spending measures.

stories.title: Samsung flags $80 billion profit on AI boom
stories.summary: Samsung Electronics has projected its quarterly profit would top 100 trillion won, a world first for a technology company, estimating a nearly nine-fold jump in third-quarter earnings as booming demand for AI chips drove strong memory sales. The world's largest memory chipmaker estimated an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won ($80.17 billion) for the July-September period, slightly ahead of an LSEG SmartEstimate of 106.1 trillion won. The forecast marks Samsung's fourth quarter of record operating profit in a row, underscoring a deepening global memory chip shortage as AI infrastructure investment outpaces supply growth, which has driven chip prices up sharply. Samsung and Micron expect the imbalance to persist into 2028, although Chinese competition and a potential slowdown in AI spending pose risks to the longer-term earnings outlook. Samsung's shares moved sideways despite flagging another record profit, slipping 0.2% in early trade versus a 0.5% fall in the benchmark KOSPI. Its share price has slumped more than 25% from a record high in June amid concerns about the durability of the AI boom. Analysts have also recently trimmed their forecasts due to the sharp appreciation of the South Korean currency, which reduces the value of dollar-denominated overseas sales when converted into local currency.

stories.title: Families protest as Nepal ends search for flood victims
stories.summary: The Nepalese government has confirmed that it is stopping the search for thousands of people who remain missing after catastrophic floods devastated the country in August. The office of Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the search and rescue operation would end. Instead, authorities will concentrate on rehabilitation and reconstruction, including restoring roads and bridges cut off by the floods, on 26 August. Families of victims have held protests and vigils in Nepal, calling for search efforts to be improved. Rescuers have recovered the bodies of at least 1,455 people, but 5,285 are missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals. "We are moving from the search and rescue phase to the search and rehabilitation phase," head of the National Emergency Operation Centre Phanindra Paudel said.

stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers welcome Drogheda United to Tallaght Stadium tonight aiming to reclaim top spot in what is developing into a thrilling SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division title race. The defending champions are chasing their sixth league crown in seven years but currently sit third in the table, albeit with only goal difference separating them, Bohemians and leaders St Patrick's Athletic. The Hoops would have been grateful for the international break coming when it did, as it gave manager Stephen Bradly a chance to reset following a dip in form from his side. A 3-2 victory over Waterford in their final game before the break was welcome but that was only their second league win since the end of July as Rovers appeared to be suffering from a major European hangover. The good news for Bradley and his side is that the league title is still very much within their grasp and a win over Drogheda would take them three points clear of the chasing pack, with the contenders all having played 32 games. With Rovers taking on Bohemians on Monday, a win for the Hoops is essential in what looks like being a pivotal few days in the title race.

stories.title: GPA and LOI academies to receive an extra €1m in Budget
stories.summary: League of Ireland academies, as well as hurling and camogie academies, are set to receive an extra €1m in funding as part of the measures introduced in Budget 2027. Another €1m has been allocated to the Gaelic Players Association (GPA). The increase in funding to League of Ireland academies in this next year's budget brings their total allocation to €4m per year - which is close to the original €4.45m sought by the FAI in advance of last year's Budget. Last year's landmark investment in League of Ireland academies had been hailed by the FAI as a "vital multi-annual investment" which can help to fund a "modern, professional academy system" in the country. The €1m allocation to the GPA falls short of the €2.8m additional investment sought by the players' body at a pre-budget submission last week, which CEO Tom Parsons said would ease cost-of-living pressures for inter-county players. The GPA described the funding as another move towards their overall target.

stories.title: CAS to hear Senegal's AFCON appeal on Thursday
stories.summary: The long-running saga over the winner of this year's Africa Cup of Nations title will move closer to resolution on Thursday when Senegal’s appeal after being stripped of the title is heard by the Court of Arbitration in Sport in Lausanne. Senegal are contesting the Confederation of African Football's decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal beating the hosts 1-0 after extra time in January's final in Rabat. Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play. Morocco failed to convert the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory. However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF's Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to Morocco. Senegal quickly followed with an appeal to CAS, which was lodged on 25 March but is only being heard on Thursday. Senegal want to be reinstated as winners and a panel will listen to arguments from Senegal, Morocco and CAF.

stories.title: Frawley and O'Shea add greater lustre to out-half debate
stories.summary: It was a tale of two Irish out-halves in last weekend's United Rugby Championship matches. Ciarán Frawley made the best first impression possible at his new club, guiding Connacht to victory over Benetton in Italy with a late try to seal the win. It is a dream start for the former Leinster utility back who has made the less conventional move west to prove a point to many people, including the Irish coaches and his former mentors at Leinster. Frawley is a talented footballer. It’s the reason he got caught in the dreaded utility role. He was so good at covering multiple positions that he never quite nailed down a sustained opportunity to make the number 10 jersey his own. When he did get his chance to perform in his preferred jersey, he had some sublime moments, mixed with some periods where he under performed. It’s not surprising that when a player in a key position fails to get enough game-time in a game management position, he fails to perform to the required level on the international stage. Though it didn’t stop him from converting a pair of memorable drop goals to beat South Africa in their own back yard. Frawley has a sizeable frame. That's why he can perform at centre and full-back. His size allows him to be a real attacking threat, taking the ball as close to the tackle line as any of the best Irish attacking out-halves. His decision making in traffic is helped by his ability to manage himself in contact. When he’s confident, there’s venom in his attacking style.

stories.title: Christy Moore exhibition opens at Irish Traditional Music Archive
stories.summary: President of Ireland Catherine Connolly has officially opened a major new exhibition exploring the life and music of singer-songwriter Christy Moore. Christy Moore: How Do Songs Live? was unveiled at the Irish Traditional Music Archive (ITMA) in Merrion Square, Dublin, last night (October 6th). The exhibition draws on materials from Moore's personal archive, donated to ITMA in 2023. The collection spans more than six decades and includes lyric notebooks, correspondence, recordings, setlists, photographs and press materials. As part of the donation, Moore recorded 188 songs in ITMA’s studio, often sharing personal stories and memories connected with them. The recordings will be available to hear as part of the exhibition. Speaking at the launch, President Connolly said: "For more than fifty years, Christy Moore has inspired generations of musicians and activists to stand in solidarity with those facing challenges and oppression. Even when it was not easy, Christy’s voice has been an example to so many of us. "Christy’s songs and music provide a vital insight and commentary on the lives of Irish people, and of the great struggles and causes of those decades. We are greatly indebted to him for all of the wonderful songs and stories he has given us, which will be treasured and learned from for decades to come."

stories.title: Strictly pro: Show changes 'not what people are used to'
stories.summary: Former Strictly Come Dancing professional Brendan Cole said the programme is "not what people are used to" since its recent shake-up, adding: "I don't think people are loving it." The hit BBC dancing competition returned for its 24th series last month with its three new presenters Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe at the helm. The stars replaced Claudia Winkleman and Tess Daly as the faces of the show, and are among a string of changes as five professional dancers also joined its latest instalment. New Zealand dancer Cole, who featured on Strictly from 2004 until 2017, discussed the changes to the flagship entertainment programme while appearing on Jeremy Vine on 5 on Wednesday. "You’ve got all the new pros. There’s no investment in them because people don’t know them yet. "They will become household names, but it’s going to take some time. You’ve also got the new hosts."

stories.title: Saoirse Ronan stuns in Louis Vuitton at Paris Fashion Week
stories.summary: Saoirse Ronan, Zendaya, and Emma Stone led the star-studded arrivals at Louis Vuitton’s futuristic show to close Paris Fashion Week. The trio were joined by French first lady Brigitte Macron at the Cour Carrée of the Louvre, where creative director Nicolas Ghesquiere had transformed the historic courtyard into a surreal racetrack. Ronan stunned in a patchwork mini skirt, a chunky red knit, and some sky-high heels for the glamorous occasion. stories.title: TikTok gave children 'placebo' safety tools, says lawsuit
stories.summary: TikTok ran an experiment on thousands of users who tried to turn ⁠on a safety feature on the platform, giving them non-functional versions of the tool, according to allegations in newly unsealed New York's lawsuit against the company. In the so-called "ghost" or placebo experiments, TikTok selected thousands of users, including teens and children, who, the lawsuit alleges, opted to use safety features like "Algo Refresh", a tool designed to reset recommendations for users seeking to escape unwanted or potentially harmful content. According to the lawsuit, those users believed they had activated the feature, but their feeds did not change, unlike users who got the fully working version. The newly unsealed allegations are part of New York Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit against the company, one of more than two dozen brought by states accusing TikTok of designing its platform to addict children and of misleading users about its safety. Many documents in state cases across the US have been sealed or heavily redacted as TikTok ‌has sought to keep details about its operations ⁠from public view. The lawsuit claims TikTok assures users that safety is a top priority and that its platform is appropriate for kids and teens, while knowingly preventing some groups of users from accessing certain safety tools, including users who had specifically sought to avoid unwanted or potentially harmful content.

stories.title: 34 garda protected disclosures in 2022 to 2026 - Minister
stories.summary: The Department of Justice received 34 protected disclosures from members and staff of An Garda Síochána between 2022 and 2026, the Minister for Justice has said. Speaking in the Dáil, Mr O'Callaghan said that in 2022 there were just three protected disclosures. That year, the Protective Disclosures Act was amended to change the process of submitting disclosures, and there were 31 disclosures in 2023. Four of these were returned by the Office of the Protected Disclosures Commissioner for examination and have been referred to "the appropriate statutory body under protected disclosure legislation". "An Garda Síochána has received 46 protected disclosures in the period 2022 to 2026. Fiosrú (the Office of the Garda Ombudsman) has received a total of 161 protected disclosures from 2022 to 2026," Minister O'Callaghan added. He defended his predecessor Helen McEntee's handling of protected disclosures, which has been heavily criticised by members of the Opposition.

stories.title: Tax changes an 'insult to workers', says Sinn Féin
stories.summary: Opposition parties have reacted strongly to the measures in Budget 2027 with Sinn Féin condemning the changes to income tax as an "insult to workers". Minister for Finance Simon Harris outlined increases to tax credits as well as the standard rate cut-off point for income tax as he delivered the Budget in the Dáil today. The Budget includes a personal income tax package worth €1.3bn, with Mr Harris explaining: "I'm increasing the standard rate cut-off point by €2,500 to €46,500, with proportionate increases for married couples and civil partners. "I'm increasing each of the main tax credits, the personal employee and earned income tax credits by €125, and I’m increasing the home carer tax credit by €100." Speaking in the Dáil this afternoon, Sinn Féin's spokesperson on finance, Pearse Doherty, said the real test of the measures will be at the end of the month when bills are paid and the Budget "fails completely". He said the Budget is about choices, and that the Government has left workers behind, adding that the "majority" of Irish workers "won't get a sniff at" the €750 tax break.

stories.title: Pre-tax losses at Clery's Quarter owner fall to €6.85m
stories.summary: Pre-tax losses at the firm that has developed Clery's Quarter on Dublin's O'Connell Street last year more than halved to €6.85m. New accounts filed by OCES Property Holdings Ltd show that the 2025 loss arose chiefly from interest payments of €7.1m. The company last year recorded an operating profit of €261,135 compared to an operating loss of €7.9m in 2024. Pre-tax losses at the company reduced as the group recorded a €353,505 gain in the value of an investment property last year compared to a €5.5m impairment in 2024 - a positive swing of €5.86m. The pre-tax loss of €6.85m last year is 55% down on the pre-tax loss of €15.27m in 2024. At the end of 2025, the group's investment property had a book value of €55.44m that comprises assets currently undergoing redevelopment.

Residents of Dundalk in Maryland, cite the usual big issues driving them to the polls for this year's midterm election in November: high gas prices, crime and immigration. "It's crazy out here. Dundalk is a Republican-leaning town in a mostly Democratic state, with President Donald Trump winning here in all three presidential elections.

stories.title: Lenihan hopeful Lee can turn Munster's fortunes around
stories.summary: Donal Lenihan says he's hopeful that Avan Lee's appointment as the Interim CEO of Munster Rugby can help the province to turn a corner after a tumultuous period. Ian Flanagan quit the role last week in the wake of a number of controversies off the pitch, most notably the decision to appoint Roger Randle as attack coach before agreeing a mutual termination of that agreement. On the field, the team have enjoyed limited success, with their last European Cup coming back in 2008, and just one addition to the trophy cabinet - a URC title in 2023 - since 2011. "There's a massive amount of frustration within the way rugby has been run within the province," he said. "You have a lot of people who've been there for a long time and I just think Avan's appointment is like drawing a line in the sand. "I'm thrilled to think that he's an independent thinker of the game. I'd like to think that he would engage with people who have a clear understanding of what rucks down here.
